# How to use Gemini Deep Research to plan a big purchase decision

> **In short:** Gemini Deep Research browses dozens of websites for you and returns a structured report with source links, so comparing big purchases like cars, appliances, or laptops stops being a full weekend of manual Googling.

Buying a new laptop, a refrigerator, or a used car usually means opening forty browser tabs and reading half of them. Gemini's **Deep Research** feature does that scrolling for you: it reads many sites, summarizes what it found, and hands you a tidy report with links back to where each claim came from. This guide walks you through using it, step by step, so the report actually answers *your* question.

## Before you start
- **A Google account** signed in on the Gemini website or the Gemini app.
- **Access to Deep Research.** It may be limited to paid Google AI plans on some accounts, so check the plan page for the latest availability before relying on it.
- **A rough idea of what you're shopping for** (a category, a budget range, and 2–3 must-haves work best — more on this in Step 2).
- **About 15–25 minutes.** Deep Research usually takes a few minutes to run, and you'll want time to read the report it returns.
- An honest expectation: the report gives you a strong starting point, but it does **not** buy the thing for you, and prices or availability can be outdated by the time you read them.

## Step 1 — Open Gemini and pick the Deep Research mode
Go to the Gemini website or open the Gemini app, then look in the chat box for a model or tool picker — usually a small dropdown above the text field. From that picker, choose the option labeled **"Deep Research."** On some accounts the option appears as a separate **Tools** button or a dedicated tab at the top of the chat. If you don't see it, it might not be enabled on your plan yet, or it could live behind a different name like **"Research"** or **"Pro."**

💬 Example: when the picker appears, click the dropdown that currently shows "Fast" or "Pro" and switch it to **Deep Research**.

You'll know it worked when the text field gains a small brief outline or "Plan" panel, and the placeholder text inside the box mentions research or sources.

## Step 2 — Describe your purchase in concrete detail
This is the most important step: the more specific your prompt, the more useful the report. Type a short paragraph that names the **item, your budget range, your must-haves, your deal-breakers, and how you'll use it.** Think of it like a one-page brief you'd give a friend who's shopping on your behalf — vague briefs produce vague reports. Avoid jargon the AI won't understand; instead, describe the thing in plain words.

💬 Example: "I need a quiet, energy-efficient dishwasher for a small kitchen, budget roughly $700–$1,000 USD, must fit a 24-inch opening and run under 45 dB. I cook most nights for two, sometimes four. Compare the top 5 models available in my country, with pros, cons, and where each one tends to be cheapest."

You'll know it worked when you see a clear "Research plan" or outline appear below your message — Gemini usually shows what it intends to search for before it starts.

## Step 3 — Approve the plan and let it run
Below the research plan, look for a button like **"Start Research"** or **"Begin."** Click it, then step away. Deep Research browses many websites in the background and writes as it goes, so the response can take **several minutes** (sometimes five, sometimes fifteen) — far longer than a normal chat reply. A progress bar or running indicator usually appears. **Do not close the tab** while it's running, or you'll lose the work.

💬 Example: hit the "Start Research" button, then make a coffee; the first draft of the report appears inline as it finishes each section.

You'll know it worked when a long, structured report lands in the chat, with section headings, bullet points, and small numbered or linked citations you can click.

## Step 4 — Read the report and click at least three sources
Don't trust any AI research report blindly. Scroll to the end of the report first and look for a **Sources** section, or for inline footnote-style numbers next to specific claims. Click at least three of those links and read the original page for a minute each, especially anything related to price, warranty, or safety. The sources tell you whether the report is repeating marketing copy or actually weighing real reviews.

💬 Example: open the report, jump to the "Sources" list at the bottom, and click the first three links — if any of them are dead, irrelevant, or from a brand's own press release, treat the matching claim with caution.

You'll know it worked when you can point to a specific source link and say, out loud, "this is where that fact came from."

## Step 5 — Ask two or three follow-up questions to narrow the field
Once the first report lands, treat it like a starting point, not the final answer. Ask Gemini to compare your top two candidates head-to-head, to look for known reliability complaints, or to translate the report into a simple "if you care most about X, choose Y; if you care about Z, choose W" decision guide. One question per message works best. If an answer feels too generic, push back: ask for specific model numbers, specific dates, or specific failure modes.

💬 Example: "Now compare models A and B from your report on noise, energy use, and reliability over five years — which one wins for a household of two who cooks daily?"

You'll know it worked when Gemini's reply is sharper and more specific than the original report, and ideally points back to the same source list.

## Step 6 — Turn the report into a personal decision checklist
Before you close the chat, ask Gemini to summarize the entire research session into a short **decision checklist** you can actually use: 3–5 finalist products, the deciding criteria for each, and the questions you still need to answer before you spend money. Copy that checklist into a note on your phone or print it. The point of the report is to leave your head clear, not crammed with new jargon.

💬 Example: "Summarize this whole conversation into a checklist: top 3 dishwashers I should see in a store, what to test in person, and what to double-check on the manufacturer's site before I buy."

You'll know it worked when you have a one-page summary in your hand that you could read in two minutes in a showroom.

## Common mistakes
- **Mistake:** Treating the report as a buy recommendation. **Fix:** It's a starting brief — the final choice is still yours, and any purchase should be confirmed against the official product page and the live price.
- **Mistake:** Skipping the sources. **Fix:** Always click at least three source links. If you can't find them, or they look unreliable, ask Gemini to redo the research with more trusted sites.
- **Mistake:** Closing the tab while research is running. **Fix:** Deep Research takes several minutes; leave the tab open until the full report appears, or you'll lose the work.
- **Mistake:** Asking a vague prompt like "best laptop under $1,000." **Fix:** Add your must-haves (size, weight, battery life, ports) and your main use (work, gaming, school) — the more detail, the better the report.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A big purchase — a car, a fridge, a laptop — stops being a weekend of forty open tabs. You get a sourced brief instead, then spend your time on the decisions that actually need a human.
- **For your business or work:** The same workflow works for buying equipment, software subscriptions, or vendor comparisons at work: ask Deep Research to compare three vendors against your checklist, then read the sources yourself before signing anything.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one purchase you've been putting off, write a two-sentence brief in Step 2, and run the report end to end. The first run is the slowest; the second one feels easy.

## Try it now
Open Gemini, switch to **Deep Research**, and paste this single sentence as your first prompt: *"I'm buying a [item] with a budget of [low]–[high], and my must-haves are [X, Y, Z]. Compare the top 5 options and end with a short decision checklist."* Fill in the brackets, hit Start Research, and read the sources before you trust any of it.
